title: How to use XLOOKUP in Excel
description: Learn how to use XLOOKUP in Excel to search ranges, return values in any direction, handle missing data, and replace VLOOKUP with hands-on practice.

args.name: lookup_value
args.text: The value you want to search for.

args.name: lookup_array
args.text: The range or column to search within.

args.name: return_array
args.text: The range or column that holds the value you want to return.

args.name: if_not_found
args.text: The text or value to display if no match is found, instead of #N/A.

args.name: match_mode
args.text: 0 for exact match (default), -1 for next smaller, 1 for next larger, or 2 for wildcard match.

args.name: search_mode
args.text: 1 to search from first to last (default), -1 to search in reverse, 2 or -2 for binary search.

sections.heading: What XLOOKUP does
sections.text: **XLOOKUP** searches a range for a specific value and returns a matching value from another range. It defaults to an exact match, so you do not need to add extra flags for everyday lookups. Here, the formula searches for the item in `A6` and returns its price.

sections.heading: Look up to the left
sections.text: Earlier functions like VLOOKUP can only return values to the right of your lookup column. With XLOOKUP, your return range can sit anywhere. Here, the formula looks up bib `425` in column B and returns the runner name from column A on its left.

sections.heading: Handle missing values cleanly
sections.text: When a lookup value does not exist, Excel normally returns a `#N/A` error. You can use XLOOKUP’s fourth argument to show a friendly fallback message instead of wrapping your formula in `IFERROR`. In this example, searching for missing order `1099` returns `Not Found`.

sections.heading: Common mistake: Mismatched range sizes
sections.text: Both `lookup_array` and `return_array` must have the exact same number of rows or columns. If you search four cells in `A2:A5` but supply five cells in `C2:C6` to return from, Excel cannot align the rows and displays a `#VALUE!` error. Always make sure your two ranges start and end on matching row numbers.
